condition.narrative: Consistent with the Article III of the SBAA [or the Supplemental Provisions to the Project Document], the responsibility for the safety and security of the Implementing Partner and its personnel and property, and of UNDP’s property in the Implementing Partner’s custody, rests with the Implementing Partner. To this end, the Implementing Partner shall: a) put in place an appropriate security plan and maintain the security plan, taking into account the security situation in the country where the project is being carried; b) assume all risks and liabilities related to the Implementing Partner’s security, and the full implementation of the security plan.

Social and environmental sustainability will be enhanced through application of the UNDP Social and Environmental Standards (http://www.undp.org/ses) and related Accountability Mechanism (http://www.undp.org/secu-srm).

Output 1:Building evidence to improve the policy environment and stimulate service provision to enhance household and community resilience 1.1: Achieved. ZRBF project supported the 2020/21 ZimVAC rural assessment processes with financial and technical assistance. It now considers differentiated impacts on women and men. The Crop and Livestock Assessments were also supported however it does not show differentiated impacts for women and men. 1.2: 10 hazard maps updated namely: 1) Drought, 2) Floods, 3)Mid-season dry spells, 4)Veld fires, 5)Cereal and livestock prices changes, 6) Landmines, 7)Crop pests and diseases, 8)Animal diseases, 9)HIV/AIDS and 10)Diarrhoeal diseases. These were mapped both at national and subnational levels that include National map, provincial maps, district, and ward maps. 1.3.: Met expectation: Despite the limitations posed by COVID 19 restrictions the MEL commitments in the annual workplan were met: -2 reflection meetings in December 2020 to review the log frame milestone and targets for 2021, - 4 remote monitoring missions were conducted virtually for the seven projects, - 4 remote MEL community of practice meetings to provide technical backstopping and troubleshoot MEL issues were held, -Two biannual SC monitoring (field trips) missions were successfully conducted one physically and the second virtually, -One virtual biannual learning event, - Quarterly consortia, development partner and steering committee performance review meetings were conducted, -PMU conducted the annual data quality assurance for all the seven -Quarterly performance reporting was produced, -ZRBF in partnership with RKH conducted OMS 3 , surveys used to inform the impact consolidation and delivery of programme strategy. 1.4: The Commercialization of the National Traditional Grains strategy document was finally finalised with technical support from PMU, RKH and leadership from MLAFWRD 1.5: 18 Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) plans were reviewed and updated for all the 18 districts as well as shared with the respective provinces for integration into development plans. - Stakeholders from the provincial and national DCP were also involved to ensure that ward and district plans are integrated within national and sub national developmental plans. - New DRM templates which link early warning, response, recovery, and contingency planning were piloted and adopted for use by all the 18 districts and this helped to strengthen DRM structures and systems in the target areas. During the review processes, action plans on new risks such Covid 19, locusts and floods were integrated into the DRM plans. Output 2: Absorptive, adaptive and transformative capacities of target communities improved 2.1: Given the reach last year (1,115, 326) and target was not adjusted the 2022 reach is met. -In 2021 achieved 1,114,532 people (426,316 males and 688216 females) were reached. -Direct project support to 210,289 households (80,437 male-headed and 129,852 female-headed households). -Currently 82% are in high intensity while 18% are intensity beneficiary categories. Overall, the ZRBF programme has 25% youth representation. Disability information from four consortia indicate that there are a total of 5190 persons living with disability from 4245 HHs. Consortia with disability data are SIZIMELE, ECRAS, BRACT and PROGRESS, with SIZIMELE having the highest number of households with a person or persons living with disability of 2868 Households. Disaggregated results by investment type: Livestock Production – 282,331 Crop production – 252,640 Community Financial Services – 86,459 Disaster Risk Management – 236,571 Non-Timber Forest Products – 10,441 Fodder Production- 85,844 Market Linkages & Value Chains – 53,217 ICT & Communication – 224,921 Infrastructure – 423,009 Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) – 246,317 Trainings – 153,213. 2.2: 307 wards reviewed and updated their DRM/resilience plans (to include covid-19 and pests) feeding into national and sub national development plans. The plans have specific Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) mitigation and adaptation action plans. 2.3: Overall, 39.1% of ZRBF beneficiaries used financial services. The COVID-19 pandemic exacerbated the challenge of access to financial services especially for women. This can be attributed to reduced flow of remittances, market disruptions, depressed demand and low disposable income due to job losses. 2.4: 307 wards with both an up-to-date DRM plans. (PROGRESS-34, BRACT-29, ECRAS-29, SIZIMELE-54, ECRIMS-50, ZVA-54, MELANA - 57). 2.5: Overall, 93.1% of ZRBF targeted households were practicing at least three climate smart agricultural production technologies during the reporting period 2.6: About 49.1% of ZRBF targeted households were practising three or more value-chain activities (on-farm & off-farm) promoted by the programme. COVID 19 also contributed to some households dropping out and not practising the promoted value chains. Somewhat “new” and unique livelihood options emerged as particularly beneficial to certain categories of ZRBF participants, such as mushroom cultivation among elderly women and social enterprises (e.g., welding, detergent making) for youth. 2.7:47,283 (22,272 female-headed, 25,011 male-headed) households were provided with access to water and basic sanitation through the main programme activities against which this indicator is scored. Majority of households were supported with rehabilitation and drilling of new boreholes under the main programme activities and the WASH grant. Target should have been revised. To be adjusted for PCR and Life of Project target. Exceeded target but met expectation given the resources that were provided in the period under review. Target to be adjusted for PCR and Life of Project target 2.8: 831 pieces of infrastructure from the main project activities were developed. Sustainable plans for guidance on governance and maintenance of the infrastructure are in place for the majority of the WASH infrastructure. Exceeded target but met expectation given the resources that were provided in the period under review. Target to be adjusted for PCR and Life of Project target. CMM mechanism was activated with limited resources in response to the flooding situation in Matobo and the outbreak of locusts in Chiredzi and Mwenezi. The CM met its objectives of rapid response and protection of development gains 3.2: Not scored 3.3: Achieved score 0.54 which is in the High Utilization category. The ZRBF Year runs from July to June OUTPUT 1: Building evidence to improve the policy environment and stimulate service provision to enhance household and community resilience 1.1 Number of risk assessments conducted, taking into account differentiated impacts on women and men. - Moderately exceeds expectations Achieved: 3 national risk assessments were conducted with both financial and technical assistance from ZRBF, namely the ZimVAC rapid assessment, Crop and Livestock (first and second round). 1.2 Number of hazards mappings developed and/or updated at subnational levels. - Updating was done and reported in 2019. These are expected to be updated again in 2021. 1.3 Robust participatory monitoring, evaluation & learning strategic framework is established, updated and operationalized. Met expectation: - A revised ToC was endorsed by Steering Committee in 2020. - Portfolio review analysis was conducted for all seven consortia partners to examine progress towards achievement of ToC/Log frame expectations and to inform the anticipated cost extension. - Quarterly consortia, development partner and steering committee performance review meetings were conducted. -Quarterly performance reporting was produced. -ZRBF conducted the second Outcome Monitoring Survey. PMU report that the results were used to design the cost extension proposals. 1.4 Number of policies, or strategies that were informed by ZRBF Evidence and Learning. Met expectation: - At the national level, no policies or strategies were informed, however a Resilience Policy Conversation Series on Accelerating the Commercialization of Traditional (Small) Grains was conducted. - 2 (local/district level) policies were influenced by ZRBF evidence and learning under the ZVA consortium. These are Mbire Natural resources management and Livestock management and control bylaws. (Bylaws are considered to be equivalent to less than one national policy or strategy.) 1.5 Number of national and sub-national DRM or development plans developed, informed by risk assessments and other evidence generated by ZRBF and taking into account gender-differentiated risk analysis. Substantially exceeded expectation A total of fifteen districts updated their DRM plans in line with improved template that was facilitated by UNDP regional office support to DCP and consortia partners. These include Nyanga, Mbire, Zvishavane, Mberengwa, Binga, Kariba, Beitbridge, Nkayi, Bubi, Umguza, Umzingwani, Mudzi and Mutoko. OUTPUT 2:Absorptive, adaptive and transformative capacities of target communities improved 2.1 Number of people supported by ZRBF to cope with the effects of climate change. Substantially exceeded expectation 1,115,326 people, 426,719 males and 688,607 were reached during the period under review through direct project support to 210 439 households (80513 male-headed and 129,926 female-headed households) Types of support ranges from trainings, crop and livestock activities, productive infrastructure development, access to water and sanitation, internal savings and lending (ISAL) groups, safety nets, and disaster risk management (DRM) activities. Overall, the ZRBF programme has 20% youth representation. Disability information from four consortia indicate that there are 3112 Households with a person or persons living with disability and a total of 3928 persons living with disability. Consortia with disability data are SIZIMELE, ECRAS, BRACT and PROGRESS, with SIZIMELE having the highest number of households with a person or persons living with disability of 2913 Households. 2.2 Number of wards with an up-to-date DRM or development plan that integrates DRM and adaptation. Exceeds expectation: 301 wards updated their DRM or DRM/resilience plans, 2.3 Percentage of people who used financial services (savings, credit, and/or insurance) in the past 12 months. (PROGRESS-24, BRACT-29, ECRAS-29, SIZIMELE-57, ECRIMS-51, ZVA-54,). 2.3 Percentage of people who used financial services (savings, credit, and/or insurance) in the past 12 months Moderately exceeded expectation: Overall, 36.6% (Males 33.5% and Females 38.9%) of ZRBF beneficiaries used financial services during the reporting period. Moderately exceeded expectation: Overall, 87.8% of ZRBF targeted households were practicing at least three climate smart agricultural production technologies during the reporting period. The percentage of males was 88.8%, of females 86.9%, of youths (15-34) 88.3% and of those aged 35 plus 87.6%. 2.6 Percentage of people who practised the value-chain activities (on-farm & off-farm) promoted by the project in the past 12 months.
